newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea offers TV debate with unions, clashes erupt.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea offers TV debate with unions, clashes erupt.

text.p: South Korea's ruling party chief on Saturday challenged union leaders to a televised debate over a controversial new labour law in a dramatic change of tack to try to turn public opinion against strikers.

But in the most violent street protest since the labour bill was rammed through parliament on December 26, about 20,000 workers clashed with riot police in central Seoul and called for the resignation of President Kim Young-sam, witnesses said.

The protesters used iron bars to rip up paving stones and fought a running battle with riot police who fired tear gas to stop them marching on Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral, where leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions are holed up.
Earlier, international labour officials visited the union leaders at their headquarters in a ramshackle tent on the grounds of the cathedral in a gesture of worker solidarity.
Their visit highlighted mounting overseas criticism of the law, which has sparked two weeks of nationwide strikes.

New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo invited union leaders to go on air for a live debate over the law, that allows companies to lay off workers and hire temporary staff to break strikes, shattering a jobs-for-life labour tradition. Lee said workers' anger largely stemmed from misunderstandings.

Public opinion is seen as a make-or-break factor in the stoppages that have closed car plants and disrupted hospitals. Unions have threatened the biggest strike in the nation's history next Tuesday and Wednesday.

Lee's offer contrasted with angry face-offs before dawn on Saturday, when police tryrce said state prosecutors were negotiating with church officials to find a way to serve the arrest warrants on the seven union leaders peacefully.
Confederation president Kwon and six deputies are camped out in Myondong a makeshift plastic tent pitched beneath a statue of the Virgin Mary.
On Saturday they too appeared to back away from violent confrontation, shaken by an attempted suicide by a Hyundai car worker on Friday who set himself on fire.

Marcello Malantacchi, secretary general of the International Metalworkers' Federation, and Guy Rider, who heads the Geneva office of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), attacked the law as an assault on fundamental rights.
"What we're doing here is adding to worldwide reaction against the offensive by the Korean government on human and trade union rights," Rider said.
